ja: נתנו לך. וגיר אלמתוכל עלי אללה לא ירי אלדניא בג'מיע מא פיהא קותא לה ובלאגא לחאג'תה, פיופר מאלה ען תאדיהֵ חקוק אללה וחקוק אלנאס מנה, פלא ישער בה חתי יתלף ענה ויבקי דונה, כקול אלכתאב פיהמא יש מפזר ונוסף עוד וחושך מיושר אך למחסור. ואלכ'אמס, אן אלמתוכל עלי אללה אנמא יתערץ' ללאסבאב פי אלדניא ליתזוד מנהא זאדא ללאכ'רה ובלאגא למעאדה, פמא צלח לה מנהא בסלאמהֵ דינה ודניאה אשתגל בה, ומא כאן פיה שבההֵ פסאד פי דינה וקצד עציאן אללה לם יתערץ' לה, לילא יסתג'לב דא עוצ'א ען אלדוא. וגיר אלמתוכל עלי אללה יאנס אלי אלאסבאב ויסכן קלבה אליהא פלא יתג'נב מנהא שיא, ויתערץ' אלי אלמד'מום ואלמחמוד מנהא, ולא יפכר פי עאקבהֵ אמרה, כקול אלחכים פיהמא חכם ירא וסר מרע וכסיל מתעבר ובוטח. ואלסאדס, אן אלמתוכל עלי אללה יצאדק ג'מיע טבקאת אלנאס, ותאנס נפוסהם אליה לאמנהם מן צ'רה, וסלאמהֵ צדורהם מן ג'התה פלא יכ'אפונה עלי עיאלהם ואמואלהם. והו איצ'א פי אמן מן ג'התהם לעלמה אן נפעה וצ'רה ליס פי יד מכ'לוק ולא פי קדרתה, פלא יכ'אף צ'רהם כמא אנה לא ירג'ו נפעהם, פאד'א אמן מנהם ואמנוא מן ג'התה צאדקהם וצאדקוה, כקול אלולי והבוטח בה' חסד יסובבנו. וגיר אלמתוכל עלי אללה לא צדיק לה ולא שפיק עליה, לאנה לא יזאל חאסדא ללנאס ובאגיא עליהם, יחסב כל נעמה צארת אליהם זאילה ענה, ואן ארזאקהם מקתטעה מן רזקה, ואן כל מא חרם מן מחבובאתה פמן קבלהם, ובאידיהם תבליגה מנאה, ואן אדרכתה אפה או מציבה פי מאל או ולד ט'ן אן ד'לך מן קבלהם, ואליהם כשף אלצ'ר ודפע
en_candidate:
**The seventh** — the one who relies on God is not saddened at the missing of a sought-after thing, nor at the loss of a beloved; he does not store up an existing thing, nor does he occupy himself with anything more than the sustenance of his day — for he does not speak with himself about what will come tomorrow, since he has no knowledge of when the conclusion of his term will be. He relies upon God for the extension of his span and the coming of his sustenance and his subsistence in it; he neither rejoices over what is to come nor grieves for it, as Scripture said: "Do not boast of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may give birth to" (Proverbs 27:1); and Ben Sira said: "Do not be anxious over the trouble of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may give birth to; tomorrow comes and he is not, and we are found troubling ourselves over a world that is not his." His worry and his sadness are only for his falling-short in what is incumbent upon him toward God of the dues; he exerts himself in fulfilling what he can of this with his outer and his inner — sensing death and the descent of fate. His fear of the descending of death upon him only adds to his emphasis and urging in provisioning himself for his next world and the slightness of his concern with preparing for this world. This is the saying of the early ones: "Repent one day before your death" (m. Avot 2:10) — and they expounded it: "Let him repent today, lest he die tomorrow; and he will be found all his days in repentance, as it is written, 'At all times let your garments be white'" (Ecclesiastes 9:8; b. Shabbat 153a).

The non-reliant on God is much-saddened by the succession of the world's misfortunes upon him: he loses his beloveds, his sought-after things slip from him, and he prepares much from the goods of the world — as if he had become safe from loss, and the fear of death had left him; as if his life would not pass away nor his term be completed and made finite. He becomes distracted from the next world and is preoccupied with this world, away from looking into the affairs of his religion, his provision, and his return. So his being-at-home in the prolongation of his term in this world is a cause of the lengthening of his hope in its affairs, and a cause of the shortening of his hope in his next world. When an admonisher admonishes him and a guide guides him, saying: "Until when will you be heedless of looking into your provision and the affairs of your return?" — he says: "When sufficiency and subsistence have been gathered for me and for all my household and dependents, until the conclusion of our matter, I shall calm my soul from the worries of the world, find leisure for fulfilling the dues of God, and look into the causes of provisioning for the day of return."

I see that I should make plain the aspects of their ignorance and error in this school in seven concepts, by which we shall uncover the magnitude of their ignorance and error — even if our discourse should grow long — for what is in this of rebuke and reproof to the people of this opinion, namely the people of pawned-pledges. For their reckoning in this is the reckoning of the merchant who, when he trades on credit with one who is not trusted with him, requires a pledge of him in his trading with him, out of fear of the slightness of his fulfilling and the slightness of his solvency and the impossibility of doing him justice.
